title: With Ames and Baron, Le Blanc opposes freedom to every necessity properly so called
source_text: XXVII. Itaque cum Amesio & Roberto Baronio dicere non veremur humani arbitrii libertatem opponi necessitati cuivis proprie dictae, nec ullum hominis actum, si stricte & proprie loquamur liberum esse, nisi ponamus in homine veram & intrinsecam potestatem aliter agendi, aut saltem actum suum suspendendi, & ab actione cessandi. Per necessitatem enim proprie dictam intelligimus illam, quae ad certam actionem sic agens determinat, ut in eo non maneat vera & intrinseca potestas non agendi, aut aliter agendi.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore with Ames & Robert Baron we do not fear to say that the liberty of human choice is opposed to any necessity properly so called, nor that any act of man, if we speak strictly & properly is free, unless we posit in man a true & intrinsic power of acting otherwise, or at least of suspending his act, & of ceasing from action. For by necessity properly so called we understand that, which so determines the agent to a certain action, that there does not remain in him a true & intrinsic power of not acting, or of acting otherwise.
pass_b_english: So, with Ames and Robert Baron, we are not afraid to say that the freedom of human choice is opposed to every necessity in the proper sense. Strictly and properly speaking, no human act is free unless we grant that man has a real, inward power to act otherwise, or at least to hold back his act and stop acting.
By necessity in the proper sense we mean what fixes the agent on a given action in such a way that no real, inward power remains in him not to act or to act otherwise.

choices.why: Le Blanc defines the phrase in the next sentence; 'in the proper sense' keeps the technical qualifier.
